title: Checkpoint: Religion Shapes the World
objective: After this level you can explain how religions have shaped law, calendars, food, art, giving, protest and science across the world.
summary: Law, calendars, food, images, giving, caste reform, nonviolence, human rights and science: religion's fingerprints across the modern world, and how ideas cross from one faith to another.

cards.headline: Chapter 9 finale: religion's fingerprints are all over the modern world.
cards.body: Law codes, calendars, menus, museum walls, protest marches and a human-rights charter. Let's lay the dates in a row, then follow one idea across borders.

cards.headline: Religion shapes the world: a timeline

events.label: Spain's Jews told to choose baptism or exile
Darwin's Origin draws both clerical praise and attack
A Catholic priest, Lemaitre, proposes the Big Bang's forerunner
UN adopts Article 18: freedom of religion
King spends five weeks in India

cards.headline: One idea, crossing borders
cards.body: Ideas don't stay home. Ahimsa, not harming living things, is shared by Jains, Hindus and Buddhists. Gandhi turned it into satyagraha, "holding onto truth", in South Africa in 1906. Decades later a Baptist minister said Christ gave him the spirit and Gandhi the method. And in 1959 King made a five-week trip to India, meeting Gandhi's family, Indian activists and Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru. Religion shapes the world most when believers carry an idea somewhere new.

cards.headline: Chapter 9 complete
learned: How religions shaped law, calendars, food and giving, and the reasons each tradition gives.
Why Ramadan moves through the seasons while Passover and Diwali stay close to theirs.
How ahimsa traveled from Jain and Hindu ethics through Gandhi to Martin Luther King Jr.
Why historians reject the idea of an endless war between science and religion.

questions.prompt: Put these moments from Chapter 9's timeline in order, from earliest to latest.
items: King spends five weeks in India
questions.explanation: Spain's Jews were told to choose in 1492, Darwin's Origin appeared in 1859, Lemaitre proposed his theory in 1927, the UN adopted Article 18 in 1948, India's constitution came in 1950, and King visited India in 1959.

questions.prompt: What does King's 1959 trip to India show about how religion shapes the world?

options.label: That nonviolence began in America
options.rationale: It began with Indian ideals of not harming.

options.label: That ideas like nonviolence travel between faiths and countries
That Gandhi learned nonviolence from King
options.rationale: The influence ran from Gandhi to King.

questions.explanation: A Jain and Hindu ideal became Gandhi's satyagraha and then King's method: ideas cross faiths and borders.

questions.prompt: Sukkot is a Jewish harvest festival dated by the Hebrew calendar. Will it drift through all the seasons like Ramadan?

options.label: Yes, by about 11 days a year
No: leap months keep it in about the same season
Yes, because it follows the Sun
options.rationale: The Hebrew calendar counts moons and adds leap months.

options.label: No, because it follows the Easter rule
options.rationale: The Easter rule is a Christian reckoning.

questions.explanation: The Hebrew calendar adds a leap month seven times in 19 years so festivals stay in season.

questions.prompt: Weigh two reasons for a food rule: God's command, or not harming living beings. Which tradition grounds its food rules mainly in the second?

options.label: Islam
options.rationale: Halal rules come from the Quran and Islamic law.

options.label: Judaism
options.rationale: Kosher rules rest on God's command in the Torah.

options.label: None of them
options.rationale: Jains avoid even root vegetables to avoid harm.

questions.explanation: Jain food rules grow from ahimsa: even root vegetables are avoided because uprooting kills the plant.

questions.prompt: This chapter found religion in law, food, giving and protest. Which part of Level 1's picture of religion does that show most?

options.label: Religion is only a set of private beliefs
options.rationale: Level 1 said religion is more than ideas.

options.label: Religion is only what scholars define it to be
options.rationale: Religion is lived, not only defined.

options.label: Religion is only about the distant past
Religious life includes moral conduct and community, not just belief

questions.explanation: Level 1: worship, moral conduct, right belief and community all make up religious life.
